title: adb: cap data_length and use lazy allocation
description:
adb: avoid unbounded reassembly allocation

The ADB dissector allocated reassembly storage based on the declared\
data_length value before payload data was processed. Since data_length\
comes from packet data, this could result in excessive memory allocation.

Replace this with incremental buffer growth using wmem_realloc() as\
payload data is copied into the reassembly buffer. This avoids\
allocating memory solely based on the declared payload length while\
preserving the existing reassembly behavior and payload validation\
logic.

Validation

Tested with a crafted capture containing data_length=0xffffffff.

Before: reassembly storage was allocated based on the declared length.

After: reassembly storage grows only as payload bytes are captured and\
copied into the reassembly buffer.

Why is this an `int`? You only cast it to a `uint32_t` later, and the function returns an `unsigned` on master, and an int which cannot be less than 0 on the earlier branches.

Good point.

I used int to match tvb_reported_length_remaining(), which can return -1 for unknown lengths. However, since the value is later compared against an unsigned length and effectively treated as non-negative, using an unsigned type (or explicitly handling the negative case first) would be clearer.

I can update this to handle the negative case explicitly and use a consistent unsigned type if preferred.

I agree that moving to the common reassembly API would be a cleaner long-term approach. I can look into that as a follow-up change once this fix is settled, especially with proper test captures to validate behavior.

I don't understand why you would need a hard max at all. When I think of lazy allocation, I still do not think of allocating all the bytes at once when receiving the first chunk, as this change still appears to do. The memory can be allocated equal in size to the first chunk and then re'alloced as necessary, or copied to a dynamically growing wmem_array_t structure, or use the methods in `epan/reassemble.h`. If you think it's too much of a change to use the reassembly API right now, I still believe a fairly simple `wmem_alloc`/`wmem_realloc` approach would involve minimal changes and prevent allocating any more than what was already present. As it is, this approach can still allocate up to your hard max even if the data is not present at all.

Something similar to:

`command_data->reassemble_data = (uint8_t *) wmem_realloc(wmem_file_scope(), command_data->reassemble_data, command_data->reassemble_data_length + chunklen);`

after truncating chunklen to the appropriate size would involve minimal changes.

@johnthacker

Thanks for the suggestion.

I've updated the implementation to remove the hard limit and switch the reassembly buffer handling to incremental growth using wmem_realloc() based on the amount of payload data actually captured. The buffer now grows as fragments are processed rather than allocating based on the declared data_length.

I kept the existing reassembly logic otherwise unchanged to keep the fix focused and minimize behavioral changes.
